The former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock has been appointed by the Australian cabinet to lead an examination into whether the country's laws sufficiently protect the human right to religious freedom. The appointment was announced in response to the national "yes" vote on marriage equality and the impending legislation.

***

This review is strategically designed to help manage a contentious political debate regarding religious amendments within a same-sex marriage bill. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull stated it was important to consider the issue of religious freedom carefully in light of the new legislative landscape surrounding marriage.

***

However, the appointment highlights a key division within the government. Treasurer Scott Morrison, while supporting the review, has insisted it is "no substitute" for immediate amendments to the marriage bill. He and others want religious protections considered at the same time as the marriage bill, while senior conservatives like Peter Dutton have suggested a separate religious freedom bill can be considered next year.

***

Prime Minister Turnbull has cautioned that many recent proposals to protect religious freedom go beyond the issue of marriage and that parliament must be wary of unintended consequences. He stated the government is particularly concerned about preventing uncertainties that could be caused by "generally worded bill of rights-style declarations" and believes any reforms should be undertaken carefully.

***

Ruddock, chosen for the role due to his past experience as Australia’s special envoy for human rights, has been asked to report his findings by March 31. Turnbull described the review as a "timely expert stocktake" that will inform the consideration of any necessary legislative reforms regarding religious freedom.
